title: Choking
blurb: Telling mild from severe airway obstruction, then back blows, abdominal or chest thrusts, and CPR if the patient becomes unresponsive.
question: While the dentist is fitting a crown, the patient suddenly sits forward, clutching their throat. They can't speak, and their coughing has become weak and silent. What do you do, and what changes if they become unresponsive?

teach.h: A blocked airway in the dental chair
teach.body: Choking happens when a foreign body blocks the airway. In dental practice that might be a crown, inlay, cotton wool roll, extracted tooth, bur or a piece of impression material, as well as food in the waiting room. Prevention matters: rubber dam, careful handling of small items and good suction all reduce the risk. If something does go back, your first job is to judge how bad the blockage is, because mild and severe obstruction are managed very differently.

teach.caption: Ask "Are you choking?" A patient who can answer out loud has a mild obstruction.

steps.label: Effective cough?
steps.sub: Yes: encourage coughing and watch closely

steps.label: Repeat 5 + 5
steps.sub: Until cleared or patient becomes unresponsive

teach.caption: Stop as soon as the obstruction clears. You don't have to give all five if one works.

teach.h: Back blows and abdominal thrusts: technique
items: Back blows: stand to the side and slightly behind. Support the chest with one hand and lean the patient well forward.
Give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand.
Abdominal thrusts: stand behind, arms around the upper abdomen. Lean the patient forward.
Place a clenched fist between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, and grasp it with your other hand.
Pull sharply inwards and upwards, up to 5 times.

teach.body: A severe obstruction can make the patient lose consciousness. Lower them carefully to the floor (or lay the dental chair flat), make sure 999 has been called, and start CPR. Chest compressions raise the pressure in the chest and may push the object out. When you open the airway for breaths, look in the mouth and remove anything you can see, but don't sweep blindly with your fingers.

teach.caption: Infants never get abdominal thrusts: their abdominal organs are unprotected and easily injured. For chest thrusts, turn the infant onto their back and use two encircling thumbs on the lower breastbone, pressing more sharply than for CPR (RCUK 2025).

children.label: Needs medical check for internal injury

children.edge: Object may be swallowed or inhaled
children.label: Dentist arranges urgent follow-up

teach.text: Don't slap the back of someone who is coughing well. A strong cough is the most effective way to clear the airway, and interfering can make things worse. Back blows and thrusts are only for an ineffective cough. And remember the order: back blows FIRST, then thrusts.

items: Severe signs: can't speak, weak or silent cough, can't breathe, clutching the throat.
Effective cough: encourage coughing and keep watching.
Ineffective cough, conscious: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts; repeat.
Infants: up to 5 back blows then up to 5 chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.
Unresponsive: 999 and start CPR. After abdominal thrusts the patient needs a medical check.

summary: You can now tell mild from severe airway obstruction, encourage an effective cough, give back blows and abdominal thrusts in the right order (chest thrusts for infants), start CPR if the patient becomes unresponsive, and arrange follow-up once the obstruction is relieved.

A.q: A patient in the waiting room starts struggling for breath while eating. Which feature best identifies a severe airway obstruction?
options: They are coughing loudly and forcefully
They can tell you they are choking
They can't speak and cough silently
Their face is red from coughing hard
A.why: An inability to speak and a weak or silent cough show a severe obstruction that needs back blows and thrusts.

whyNot.0: A loud, forceful cough is effective, so this is mild obstruction.
whyNot.1: Being able to speak means air is moving: mild obstruction.
whyNot.3: Redness from coughing hard suggests an effective cough.

A.q: A conscious adult has a severe airway obstruction with an ineffective cough. What should you do first?
options: Sweep the mouth with a finger
A.why: For a conscious adult with an ineffective cough, give up to 5 back blows first, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts.

whyNot.0: Abdominal thrusts come after back blows, if back blows haven't worked.
whyNot.2: CPR is started if the patient becomes unresponsive.
whyNot.3: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further down.

A.q: A choking patient becomes unresponsive. What should you do?
options: Keep giving back blows standing up
Give abdominal thrusts on the floor
Wait for the object to pass on its own
Lie them down, call 999 and start CPR
A.why: RCUK: if a choking patient becomes unconscious, call for an ambulance and start CPR.

whyNot.0: An unresponsive patient can't be supported standing; they need CPR.
whyNot.1: CPR is the recommended action for an unconscious choking patient, not floor thrusts.
whyNot.2: Waiting means no oxygen reaching the brain.

B.q: A patient chokes on a cotton wool roll but is coughing hard and can still talk. What should you do?
options: Give up to 5 back blows at once
Lie them flat and start CPR
B.why: An effective cough is the best way to clear a mild obstruction: encourage coughing and watch for it becoming ineffective.

whyNot.1: Back blows are for an ineffective cough; they can interfere with a good one.
whyNot.2: Thrusts are only for severe obstruction after back blows.
whyNot.3: CPR is for an unresponsive patient, not one who is talking.

B.q: Where should you place your fist when giving abdominal thrusts to an adult?
options: On the lower half of the breastbone
Between navel and bottom of breastbone
Below the navel, over the lower abdomen
Between the shoulder blades at the back
B.why: The fist goes on the upper abdomen, between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, and you pull sharply inwards and upwards.

whyNot.0: The lower breastbone is where you compress for CPR (or chest thrusts in infants).
whyNot.2: Below the navel is too low to push air up from the lungs.
whyNot.3: Between the shoulder blades is where back blows are given.

B.q: A 9-month-old baby is choking and can't cry or cough effectively. After up to 5 back blows, what comes next?
B.why: Infants get up to 5 back blows then up to 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are not used under 1 year.

whyNot.0: Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant's unprotected abdominal organs.
whyNot.1: Blind sweeps can push the object further in.
whyNot.3: Holding by the legs isn't the recommended technique; use head-down along your forearm.

C.q: A patient is clutching their throat, unable to speak and making silent efforts to breathe. What should you recognise first?
options: An asthma attack needing an inhaler
A faint that will settle if they lie flat
C.why: Clutching the throat, being unable to speak and silent breathing efforts are classic signs of severe airway obstruction.

whyNot.0: Someone panicking can usually still speak and breathe audibly.
whyNot.2: Asthma causes wheeze, and the patient can usually speak in short sentences.
whyNot.3: A faint causes loss of consciousness, not silent efforts to breathe.

C.q: After 5 back blows have failed to clear a severe obstruction in a conscious adult, what is the next step?
C.why: If back blows fail, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts, then keep alternating 5 and 5.

whyNot.0: After 5 back blows, the next step is abdominal thrusts, then back to back blows.
whyNot.1: Chest compressions are for an unresponsive patient.
whyNot.2: Rescue breaths are part of CPR, not for a conscious choking patient.

C.q: Abdominal thrusts cleared a patient's airway and they now feel well. What should happen next?
options: They should be checked by a doctor
They can carry on with treatment
They should have a drink and go home
Nothing, as the airway is now clear
C.why: Abdominal thrusts can cause internal injury, so anyone who has received them should be medically assessed.

whyNot.1: Continuing treatment ignores the risk of internal injury.
whyNot.2: Sending them home without assessment misses possible injury.
whyNot.3: A clear airway doesn't rule out injury from the thrusts.

reteach.title: Let the cough do the work
reteach.question: The body has its own tool for clearing the airway. When should you help it, and when should you leave it alone?

blocks.body: A strong cough is the most powerful way to blow an object out, far better than anything you can do from outside. So if the patient is coughing well and can talk, your job is to encourage them and watch. Only when the cough fails (weak, silent, can't speak) do you step in: back blows to jolt the object loose, then thrusts to squeeze air up from the lungs like popping a cork. If they collapse, CPR takes over.

blocks.text: Infants: back blows then CHEST thrusts. Children and adults: back blows then ABDOMINAL thrusts.

explain.body: Severe obstruction: the patient can't speak, the cough is weak or silent, they can't breathe and may clutch their throat. Mild: they can talk, cough and breathe.

test.q: Which sign suggests a MILD airway obstruction?
test.why: A loud, strong cough means air is moving: mild obstruction.

whyNot.0: A silent cough shows severe obstruction.
whyNot.1: Being unable to speak shows severe obstruction.
whyNot.3: Turning blue shows a lack of oxygen from severe obstruction.

explain.body: Lean the patient well forward, supporting the chest. Give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking after each one.

items.label: back blows, between the shoulder blades

test.q: Why should the patient lean well forward during back blows?
options: So the object moves out, not down
So they can see what you are doing
To stop them coughing during blows
test.why: Leaning forward lets gravity help the dislodged object come out of the mouth rather than fall further down.

whyNot.1: Seeing what you're doing isn't the reason.
whyNot.2: Abdominal thrusts are a separate step.
whyNot.3: Coughing helps; you don't want to stop it.

explain.body: Stand behind, fist between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, other hand over it. Pull sharply inwards and upwards up to 5 times. Afterwards the patient needs a medical check for internal injury.

test.q: In which direction do you pull during an abdominal thrust?
test.why: Pulling inwards and upwards pushes air up from the lungs to force the object out.

whyNot.0: Straight down wouldn't push air towards the airway.
whyNot.2: Sideways force doesn't help clear the airway.
whyNot.3: Downwards pushes away from the airway.

explain.body: If the patient becomes unresponsive, call 999 and start CPR. For infants, use head-down back blows along your forearm then chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.

test.q: Why are abdominal thrusts not used for choking infants?
options: Back blows always work in infants
test.why: An infant's abdominal organs are unprotected and easily injured, so chest thrusts are used instead.

whyNot.0: Infants do choke, often on small objects or food.
whyNot.1: Infants are held head-down along the forearm for back blows.
whyNot.2: Back blows don't always work, which is why chest thrusts follow.
